newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S., in shift, backs commercial space industry.
newsitem.headline: U.S., in shift, backs commercial space industry.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, in a policy shift, has been actively supporting the U.S. commercial space industry, left by previous administrations to win contracts on its own, a senior U.S. official said on Friday.

The booming worldwide market for civilian satellites, launchers and ground equipment is expected to surpass $30 billion this year -- a ten-fold increase from a decade ago, with sustained growth expected over the next five years.
Politics as well as price and quality can play a key role in clinching the massive contracts.
"We think it's absolutely necessary for the commercial space industry to flourish to its maximum," said Ellis Motter, acting deputy secretary of commerce.

"Previous administrations held to an ideological fix that the government could not touch anything. That may have made some sense in some distant past, but in the global economic competition, governments have to work in partnership with industry," Motter said in an interview at the Paris airshow.
"Certainly all governments I know of in Europe and elsewhere are doing that and the U.S. has to do that too," he said.

Launch companies have made a strong comeback since the mid 1980s when the U.S. commercial launch programme was dealt a devastating blow by the Challenger shuttle disaster and the Reagan administration's decision to exclude commercial payloads from the space shuttle programme.
Expendable U.S. rocket production had all but stopped and contracts went rapidly to Europe's Arianespace which dominated the market for nearly a decade.

Now U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin Corp says it has pulled even in market share with Ariane in its International Launch Services division (ILS), which launches the Atlas rocket from Flordia and Russia's Proton rocket from the Baikanour Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
The United States signed a bilateral agreement with Russia in 1993 which pemits it to launch 20 commercial payloads up to the year 2000.
"This agreement permitted Russia to enter the market for international space launches. It provided both pricing and quantity guidelines to encourage market behaviour," said Motter.
"We think it gives us a good framework where Russia can utilise its facilities in a way that will not set up an unfair pricing system that is unfair to western launch providers."

As recently as three years ago, companies estimated only 20 heavy commercial satellites would be launched annually. This figure has rocketed with heavy demand particularly in the booming Asia-Pacific rim countries.

"I think we are going to have a sustained period of growth over the next five years. It will then depend on the development of business in Asia and other places," said Mike Henshaw, president of Lockeed Martin's Missiles & Space division.
